extracted.intended_audience: lawmakers, regulators, legal scholars, and policymakers interested in technology governance (AI, platforms, emerging tech)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance for how legislatures, agencies, and courts should (and should not) respond to emerging technologies; argues for defaulting to general legal doctrines and judicial adaptation rather than prophylactic, technology-specific statutes. Emphasizes institutional limits, timing, and design choices (rules vs. standards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Default to Generality
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawmakers should 'default to generality.' The law's virtue is its capacity to apply generally across cases, actors, and epochs; property, tort, and contract doctrines are capacious enough to accommodate technological change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid bespoke statutes for each new technology (e.g., social media, generative AI, targeted advertising). Favor abstract, general rules that operate by relationships rather than by technology categories. The desire for granularity is understandable but risks obsolescence and inflexibility; general rules endure in a dynamic world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional Humility
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the epistemic limits of legislatures, regulators, and experts; policymakers cannot reliably predict the downstream consequences of new technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because knowledge is dispersed, tacit, and contextual (Hayekian knowledge problem), regulators should exercise restraint. Policymakers should avoid acting as if they can anticipate downstream effects; the costs of mistaken precaution can outweigh the risks of permissive treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let Courts Do Their Work
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary, through case-by-case adjudication and accretional decision-making, is the appropriate primary mechanism to integrate new facts and apply existing doctrines to novel technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow courts to adapt doctrines like trespass, negligence, products liability, fiduciary duty, misrepresentation, and fraudulent inducement to new contexts rather than commanding forward-looking legislatures to create technology-specific rules. Litigation is retrospective, fact-sensitive, and limited—qualities that make judicial adaptation preferable to prophylactic statutory design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let Innovation Proceed by Default (Permissionless Innovation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovation should be presumptively allowed; regulation should follow demonstrable harm rather than pre-authorizing or forbidding new technologies in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a jurisprudential allocation of burdens: innovators are allowed unless and until they cause demonstrable, compensable harm. This sequence preserves experimentation, avoids entrenching incumbents, and prevents lost possibilities that come from precautionary ex ante controls. Use ex post remedies (tort, contract, consumer protection) when harm materializes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer Standards over Rules in Fast-Moving Domains
rubrics_metrics.description: When lawmakers adopt standards (broad principles like reasonableness, good faith, fairness) rather than highly specific rules, the legal system remains more adaptable to change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules give ex ante certainty but are costly to promulgate and update and can ossify; standards postpone specificity to decisionmakers who can consider facts as they unfold. In contexts of rapid technological change, standards and common-law adjudication are typically better suited than rigid, technology-specific rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Premature, Overly Specific Legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislatures should resist the impulse to enact prophylactic, technology-specific statutes aimed at hypothetical or speculative threats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Premature lawmaking often codifies guesses, locks in early designs, stifles experimentation, and can produce brittle regimes that become outdated. Policymakers should question whether new law is necessary or whether existing general doctrines suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of Regulatory Capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawmaking and administrative processes are prone to being shaped by organized interests—particularly incumbent firms in tech—which can distort policy toward those incumbents' benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that concentrated benefits and diffuse costs favor industry influence. Avoid regulatory architectures that create new points of entry for power or that make regulated entities the primary sources of expertise and rule design; consider institutional designs that mitigate capture risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Ossification of Rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural accumulation around rulemaking (complex procedures, review mandates) can make administrative law slow, legally risky, and unwilling or unable to update rules in light of new circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive procedural burdens push agencies away from deliberative rulemaking toward guidance documents and informal enforcement actions, reducing transparency and democratic accountability and increasing the risk that law becomes outdated and incoherent. Policymakers should weigh these procedural costs when designing regulatory interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Existing General-Purpose Doctrines to Address Harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Many harms produced by new technologies—fraud, harms to person or property, breaches of duty—can be addressed through established doctrines (tort, contract, property, consumer protection) rather than novel statutory architectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply and where necessary modestly refine common-law doctrines to new fact patterns instead of creating new, technology-specific rules. This leverages the law's stability and adaptability without imposing brittle, bespoke regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design Policy with Attention to Sequencing and Incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy should be sequenced so regulation follows observable harms, and design choices should consider incentives effects—e.g., whether regulation will entrench incumbents or raise compliance costs that exclude small entrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer remedies and liability structures that address realized injuries rather than pre-emptive bans. Evaluate proposals for likely distributional effects (who bears compliance costs) and whether they will channel innovation into less-regulated or less-beneficial domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist Techno-Legal Exceptionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat each new technology as sui generis requiring radical reengineering of the legal system; instead, check whether the core problems differ materially from those the law already handles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the issue is a novel type of harm or a familiar harm in a new guise. If the latter, prefer existing institutions and doctrines; reserve statutory innovation for genuinely new problems that cannot be addressed by the general law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor Modest, General, and Rare Legal Change
rubrics_metrics.description: When legal change is necessary, it should be modest in scope, broadly framed, and infrequent—preserving abstraction, stability, and resistance to fads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative interventions should avoid fine-grained technical specifications and instead make general adjustments that leave space for courts and markets to work. Excessively frequent or detailed statutory tinkering risks creating brittle legal frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider Non-Regulatory and Market-Based Alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Private ordering mechanisms (e.g., insurance, liability rules, contractual governance) and regulatory sandboxes can sometimes address risks without broad statutory intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where appropriate, use insurance regimes, sandboxes, or private law tools as alternatives or complements to public regulation to internalize harms and permit experimentation while preserving accountability.
